Reproducing Moore et al. (2025) from dandiset 001699¶

Paper. Moore N, Duszkiewicz AJ, Asiminas A, Dudchenko PA, Peyrache A, Wood ER (2025). Age-dependent alterations in the head-direction signal in a rat model of Fragile X Syndrome. bioRxiv. doi:10.1101/2025.01.09.632139. This attempt used the full text of version 1 (9 January 2025), the version the dandiset links and whose title the target names. A revised version 2 (7 January 2026, "Altered developmental profile of the cortical head-direction signal in a rat model of Fragile X Syndrome") was also read; its Methods are used only where version 1 is silent (the Bayesian decoder, the speed smoothing), and its numbers are compared in the attempt record.

Data. DANDI:001699, version 0.260917.2322, streamed from the archive. The paper cites no version (its Data Availability says the data will be released at publication). Two versions are published, 0.260917.2313 and 0.260917.2322, nine minutes apart; the data check below shows that their assets are the same files, and the metadata differ only in the title, description and study target. The most recent published version is pinned, as the protocol asks when no version is cited and no earlier one matches the paper better.

Code. The dandiset links the lab's package woodcode (https://github.com/Wood-Dudchenko-lab/woodcode, read at commit 61ee1784ef8bdeed1befa4d2dd2dd71dc8befd60). It holds general functions (waveform trough-to-peak, Skaggs information, Rayleigh vector length, a Poisson decoder, loading NWB files) and not the paper's analysis, which the Methods say was run in Matlab and R. Where the Methods leave a choice open and woodcode settles it (the channel used for trough-to-peak, positive waveforms, circular smoothing) the helper module hdfx.py follows woodcode; its docstring lists where each parameter comes from.

with DandiAPIClient() as client:
    ds = client.get_dandiset(hdfx.DANDISET_ID, hdfx.DANDISET_VERSION)
    raw = ds.get_raw_metadata()
    summary = raw["assetsSummary"]
    print("name:", raw["name"])
    print("archive summary: subjects", summary["numberOfSubjects"], "| files", summary["numberOfFiles"],
          "| species", [s["name"] for s in summary["species"]],
          "| variables", summary["variableMeasured"])
    print("related resources:", [(r.get("name"), r.get("relation"), r.get("url")) for r in raw["relatedResource"]])
    print("about:", [(a["name"], a["schemaKey"], a["identifier"]) for a in raw.get("about", [])])
    versions, asset_age = {}, []
    for v in ("0.260917.2313", "0.260917.2322"):
        d = client.get_dandiset(hdfx.DANDISET_ID, v)
        versions[v] = set()
        for a in d.get_assets():
            md = a.get_raw_metadata()
            versions[v].add((a.path, a.size, md["digest"]["dandi:dandi-etag"]))
            if v == hdfx.DANDISET_VERSION and a.path.endswith(".nwb"):
                subj = [w for w in md.get("wasAttributedTo", []) if w.get("schemaKey") == "Participant"]
                asset_age.append({"path": a.path, "asset_metadata_age": subj[0].get("age", {}).get("value") if subj else None})
        print(f"version {v}: {len(versions[v])} assets, title {d.get_raw_metadata()['name']!r}")
    print("same assets (path, size, etag) in both published versions:",
          versions["0.260917.2313"] == versions["0.260917.2322"])
asset_age = pd.DataFrame(asset_age).sort_values("path")
print("\nage in the archive's asset metadata (derived by the archive from the date of birth):")
print(asset_age.to_string(index=False))

The two published versions hold the same 98 assets (36 NWB files and 62 videos); they differ in title and description only, so the choice between them does not change the analysis. The archive counts 24 subjects of Rattus norvegicus, as the files do. Its about field lists "Fmr1 protein, rat" as an anatomy term with the MeSH identifier of Fragile X Syndrome (D005600), a metadata error.

Every file has a units table with only spike_times, waveform_mean, electrode_group and sampling_rate: no cell type, quality metric or depth, so the paper's cell selection is recomputed from the waveforms and spike trains. No NWB file sets the subject's age; the archive's asset metadata give an age derived from the date of birth (printed above). Subjects H3023 and H3026 have dates of birth a year after their recordings, so the archive gives them negative ages (P-366D to P-344D), a metadata error; their age group is taken from their other properties below. The session description of every file mentions a cue rotation, which version 1 of the paper does not describe; most files hold a third tracked session after the second, which is not used. One unit in H3023 (session 210812) has spike times out of order, a format error; the helper sorts them. Every file holds histology images (acquisition/histology_images, printed above), including the four whose asset names lack +image; none marks the probe tract or the postsubiculum, so figs1d-probe-in-posub is blocked.

def counts(df, age_col, geno_col):
    g = df.groupby([age_col, geno_col])
    return pd.DataFrame({"rats": g.subject.nunique(), "recordings": g.size(), "units": g.n_units.sum(),
                         "min_units": g.n_units.min(), "max_units": g.n_units.max()})

With the archive's labels no grouping reproduces the paper's counts (406 units in 7 juvenile WT rats, 372 in 5 juvenile Fmr1-/y, 543 in 6 adult WT, 507 in 6 adult Fmr1-/y). If H3026 is a juvenile Fmr1-/y rat (the archive says WT, and gives it a birth date after its recording) and H3029 a juvenile WT rat (its birth date, the same as H4830's, makes it 97 days old), three of the four groups match the paper exactly in units and rats. H3026's 83 units in one recording is also the top of the paper's range for juveniles. H3026 and H3029 are the only rats recorded with 64-channel probes, which fits their being a later juvenile cohort. This is consistent with the data but not proven by it; the genotype of H3026 cannot be checked from the files. The main grouping uses it, and the claims show the archive's labels as a variant. The archive's genotype labels are recorded as a finding.

H4825's file holds H4824's recording: the same 88 units with identical waveforms, spike counts and spike times up to 1248 s (the end of H4825's first epoch), after which H4825's spike and tracking times are shifted piece by piece onto H4825's own epoch table and clipped at its end (many spikes then share the last spike time, which makes 87 of 88 units look contaminated). This recording is counted once, as H4824, and H4825 has no data of its own in the dandiset. No other pair of files shares unit and spike counts.

The paper describes two 20 min exploration sessions separated by 90 min of sleep. The epochs and processing/tasks tables do not always say which interval is which: in H3001 (200202) task epoch 1 is called wake but spans 94 min with no tracking, and tracking starts in epoch 2; in H3026 (211003) epoch 1 spans 112 min, waking and sleep together; H4823 has a single epoch for the whole recording and no sleep task. The exploration sessions are therefore taken from the tracking itself (helper exploration_sessions): the first tracking block of at least 10 min, and the first such block starting at least 60 min later, each cut to its first 20 min, the paper's session length. This gives sessions of 18.7 to 20.0 min (H4825 aside) before and after the sleep in every recording but two, which have one session: in H3019 210618-1 it is the session before the sleep, and in H3001 200202, where the first epoch has no tracking, it is the session after the sleep. Juvenile files have one to three tracking frames whose timestamp does not increase; those frames are dropped.

files in centimetres: 34; frames with y exactly 0 per file: 1 to 1; with x exactly 0: 0 to 0

Position is stated in centimetres, and in 34 files spans about 72 to 83 cm on each axis, consistent with the 73 cm arena seen from above. In each of these files exactly one frame has y equal to 0 and none has x equal to 0, so the y positions were shifted to start at 0; missing tracking is stored as NaN, not as 0. In two files (H3015 210417 and H4823 221108) it spans 300 and 700 units, so it is in pixels although the file says centimetres (a metadata error); their head direction runs from -pi to pi where the other files run from 0 to 2 pi, and they hold tracking through the sleep. For these two files the scale is set so that the x extent of the exploration tracking equals the arena's 73 cm (4.1 and 9.5 pixels per cm). Tracking is at 40 Hz in juveniles and 40.7 Hz in adults, consistent with the Methods' 40 Hz. H3029 is tracked at 40.7 Hz like the adults, so it was recorded on the adult rig.

The trough-to-peak durations are bimodal with the trough between 0.40 and 0.47 ms, consistent with the Methods' thresholds (0.5 ms for juveniles, 0.4 ms for adults). The unit totals match the paper's counts of recorded units (see unit-counts), so the files hold all curated units, not only the putative excitatory ones. The Methods say units with a contamination score "below 0.5" were excluded; almost every unit is below 0.5, so this is read as "above 0.5", which removes few units.

# frame_counts on frames that are not contiguous (speed-filtered), on synthetic spikes
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
t_all = np.arange(0, 600, 0.025)
keep = rng.random(len(t_all)) > 0.3            # frequent one-frame and longer gaps
t_sel = t_all[keep]
sp = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 600, 20000))
expected = np.histogram(sp, np.r_[t_all - 0.0125, t_all[-1] + 0.0125])[0][keep]
got = hdfx.frame_counts([sp], t_sel, 0.025)[0]
print(f"spikes in the kept frames: expected {expected.sum()}, counted {int(got.sum())}; "
      f"frames with a wrong count: {int(np.sum(got != expected))} of {len(t_sel)}")
assert np.array_equal(got, expected)

spikes in the kept frames: expected 13843, counted 13843; frames with a wrong count: 0 of 16746

frame_counts counts each tracking frame on its own window, so frames kept by a speed filter need not be contiguous; on synthetic spikes it counts every spike of the kept frames. The first round of this attempt cut frames at gaps and lost or misplaced spikes there.

peak within 0.2 s of zero in 34 of 35 recordings; zero-lag information at least 1.5 times that at +-60 s in 32
recordings where the clock is not established (ratio below 1.5): ['H3006 200314_1', 'H3006 200314_2', 'H3015 210416_2']

Spikes and tracking share a clock: with the spikes shifted against the head direction, HD information peaks within 0.2 s of zero lag in 34 of 35 recordings and falls towards its floor at 60 s. In H3023 210812 the information is nearly flat (0.019 to 0.023 bits/spike between -2 and 2 s) and peaks at -0.5 s. In three recordings (H3006 200314-1 and 200314-2, H3015 210416-2), whose cells are weakly tuned, the information at zero lag is less than 1.5 times that at 60 s. For these four a shared clock is consistent with the data but not shown.

The sleep stages are consistent with the pseudo-EMG: its median is lower in REM than in wake in all 36 files, and at or below its NREM median in 31. A few REM intervals overlap the tracking blocks of the exploration sessions (counted above, up to 4 in H3015 210416-2 and 3 in H4822). The REM analyses use every REM interval, as the claims' criterion says, and show the result with those intervals left out as a variant.

Tables used by the claims¶

cells has one row per cell (a putative excitatory unit with contamination at most 0.5 and at least 100 spikes in session 1) and recording; recs has one row per recording. H4825 is left out. The archive grouping variant uses the archive's genotype, and the archive's age group where the birth date gives one (H3029 is then adult and its cells are selected with the adult threshold).

def lme_variants(value, age, higher="KO", log_ok=True, uniform_col=None, extra=None):
    '''The LME test and its variants for one cell measure in one age group.'''
    d = cells[cells.age_group == age]
    rows = []
    def add(name, df, col=value, log=False):
        coef, p, n = hdfx.lme_lrt(df, col, log=log)
        rows.append({"test": name, "n": n, "coef_KO_minus_WT": coef, "p": p})
    add("LME (main)", d)
    if log_ok:
        add("LME on log values", d, log=True)
    if not d.first_day.all():
        add("LME, first day of each rat", d[d.first_day])
    add("LME, archive labels", cells_arch[cells_arch.age_group == age])
    if age == "juvenile":
        add("LME, H3026 left out", d[d.subject != "H3026"])
    if uniform_col:
        add("LME, uniform occupancy (v2)", d, col=uniform_col)
    if extra is not None:
        add(*extra)
    ko, wt = d.loc[d.genotype == "KO", value].dropna(), d.loc[d.genotype == "WT", value].dropna()
    mw = stats.mannwhitneyu(ko, wt)
    rows.append({"test": "Mann-Whitney on cells", "n": len(ko) + len(wt), "coef_KO_minus_WT": ko.median() - wt.median(), "p": mw.pvalue})
    am = d.groupby(["animal", "genotype"])[value].mean().reset_index()
    tt = stats.ttest_ind(am.loc[am.genotype == "KO", value], am.loc[am.genotype == "WT", value])
    rows.append({"test": f"t-test on animal means, t({len(am) - 2}) = {tt.statistic:.2f}", "n": len(am),
                 "coef_KO_minus_WT": am.loc[am.genotype == "KO", value].mean() - am.loc[am.genotype == "WT", value].mean(), "p": tt.pvalue})
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    summ = d.groupby("genotype")[value].agg(["count", "median", "mean", "min", "max"])
    per_animal = d.groupby(["genotype", "animal"])[value].agg(["count", "median", "mean"])
    return out, summ, per_animal


def show(value, age, **kw):
    out, summ, per_animal = lme_variants(value, age, **kw)
    print(f"{value}, {age}: cells by genotype")
    print(summ.round(3).to_string())
    print("\nper rat")
    print(per_animal.round(3).to_string())
    print("\ntests")
    print(out.round(4).to_string())
    return out


def corr(age, x, y, df=None):
    d = (cells if df is None else df)
    d = d[d.age_group == age].dropna(subset=[x, y])
    rows = []
    for g in ("WT", "KO"):
        e = d[d.genotype == g]
        r, p = stats.pearsonr(e[x], e[y])
        f = e[e.first_day]
        rows.append({"genotype": g, "cells": len(e), "rats": e.animal.nunique(), "r": r, "p": p,
                     "spearman": stats.spearmanr(e[x], e[y])[0],
                     "r_first_day": stats.pearsonr(f[x], f[y])[0], "cells_first_day": len(f),
                     "x_range": (round(e[x].min(), 3), round(e[x].max(), 3)), "y_range": (round(e[y].min(), 3), round(e[y].max(), 3))})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def scatter(age, x, y, xlabel, ylabel):
    """Per-cell scatter of y against x by genotype, cells of later days marked."""
    d = cells[cells.age_group == age].dropna(subset=[x, y])
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    for k, g in enumerate(("WT", "KO")):
        e = d[d.genotype == g]
        for first, mk, lab in ((True, "o", "first day"), (False, "x", "later day")):
            f = e[e.first_day == first]
            ax[k].scatter(f[x], f[y], s=8, marker=mk, alpha=0.6, label=lab)
        hi = max(d[x].max(), d[y].max())
        ax[k].plot([0, hi], [0, hi], c="0.6", lw=0.8)
        ax[k].set_title(f"{age} {g}")
        ax[k].set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax[0].set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax[0].legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    print(f"plotted ranges: {x} {d[x].min():.3f} to {d[x].max():.3f}; {y} {d[y].min():.3f} to {d[y].max():.3f} (no point outside the axes)")
    e = d.assign(diff=(d[y] - d[x]).abs()).sort_values("diff", ascending=False)
    print("the ten cells farthest from the diagonal:")
    print(e[["subject", "session", "genotype", "unit", "first_day", x, y, "diff"]].head(10).round(3).to_string())

unit-counts¶

406 units were recorded from 7 juvenile WT rats and 372 from 5 juvenile Fmr1-/y rats; 543 units from 6 adult WT rats and 507 from 6 adult Fmr1-/y rats.

exc_units = pd.Series({(r["meta"]["subject"], r["meta"]["session_id"]): r["main"]["rec"]["n_exc_ttp"] for r in results if r["main"] is not None})
def table(df, age_col, geno_col, reading):
    rows = []
    for (age, geno), (eu, er) in expected.items():
        d = df[(df[age_col] == age) & (df[geno_col] == geno)]
        n = d.n_units.sum() if reading == "a" else sum(exc_units.get((s, ss), 0) for s, ss in zip(d.subject, d.session_id))
        rows.append({"group": f"{age} {geno}", "units": n, "paper_units": eu, "units_ok": abs(n - eu) <= 0.1 * eu,
                     "rats": d.subject.nunique(), "paper_rats": er, "rats_ok": abs(d.subject.nunique() - er) <= 0.1 * er})
    t = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    t["group_ok"] = t.units_ok & t.rats_ok
    return t

Result: partially reproduced. Counting every unit of each recording once, the juvenile WT (406 units, 7 rats), juvenile Fmr1-/y (372, 5) and adult WT (543, 6) groups match the paper exactly, with H3026 taken as Fmr1-/y and H3029 as a juvenile. The adult Fmr1-/y group has 440 units in 5 rats against 507 in 6, because H4825's file holds H4824's recording. Counting H4825's file as a recording of its own gives 528 units in 6 rats, within the tolerance, but it counts one recording twice. As putative excitatory units no group matches, and with the archive's labels no group matches.

Result: partially reproduced. Counting all units, the juvenile recordings hold 8 to 83, as the paper says, and the adult ones 55 to 114, so the adult minimum differs. As putative excitatory units by trough-to-peak duration, the ranges are 5 to 50 (juvenile) and 30 to 81 (adult). The paper's juvenile range and adult maximum are counts of all units, and its adult minimum is the count of putative excitatory units in H4822, so the reported ranges mix the two readings.

figs1c-juvenile-behaviour-similar and figs2c-adult-behaviour-similar¶

Juvenile (and adult) Fmr1-/y and WT rats do not differ in the time spent inactive, the time spent in the centre of the arena, or the speed while active.

def behaviour(age):
    d = recs[recs.age_group == age].groupby(["subject", "genotype"])[["inactive", "centre", "active_speed"]].mean().reset_index()
    rows = []
    for col in ("inactive", "centre", "active_speed"):
        ko, wt = d.loc[d.genotype == "KO", col], d.loc[d.genotype == "WT", col]
        t = stats.ttest_ind(ko, wt)
        rows.append({"measure": col, "WT_mean": wt.mean(), "KO_mean": ko.mean(), "WT_range": (round(wt.min(), 3), round(wt.max(), 3)),
                     "KO_range": (round(ko.min(), 3), round(ko.max(), 3)), "df": len(d) - 2, "t": t.statistic, "p": t.pvalue})
    return d, pd.DataFrame(rows)
for age in ("juvenile", "adult"):
    d, t = behaviour(age)
    print(f"{age}: per rat (fractions of tracked time; speed in cm/s)")
    print(d.round(3).to_string())
    print(t.round(4).to_string(), "\n")

Result: figs1c-juvenile-behaviour-similar reproduced; figs2c-adult-behaviour-similar reproduced. In juveniles no measure differs by t-test on rat means at 0.05: time inactive p = 0.39, time in the centre p = 0.093, speed while active p = 0.063 (Fmr1-/y 5.74 against WT 4.88 cm/s). The active speed differs with the first day of each rat alone (p = 0.034), so the absence of a speed difference is fragile; with thresholds of 2 cm/s and a centre disc of a third of the diameter, p = 0.25, 0.11 and 0.26. In adults none differs (p = 0.91, 0.355 and 0.70).

Result: figs1-juvenile-cell-metrics-similar reproduced; figs2-adult-cell-metrics-similar reproduced. No main LME test finds a genotype effect on contamination, mean rate, peak rate or vector length (juveniles p = 0.11 to 0.72; adults p = 0.10 to 0.34). Mann-Whitney tests on cells, which ignore the rat, find differences in juvenile mean rate (p = 0.038) and vector length (p = 0.0001), and in adult mean rate, peak rate and vector length (p = 0.022, 0.0026 and 0.0032).

fig1ef-juvenile-sharper-tuning¶

Result: partially reproduced. HD information is higher in juvenile Fmr1-/y cells than in WT cells (median 0.596 against 0.189 bits/spike; LME p = 0.030), and stays so with the first day of each rat alone (p = 0.035), but not on log values (p = 0.12), with uniform occupancy as in version 2 (p = 0.081), on rat means (t(10) = 2.11, p = 0.061), with H3026 left out (p = 0.072) or with the archive's labels (p = 0.23). The half-width does not differ (median 50 against 62 degrees; LME p = 0.54).

Result: not reproduced. With the sessions as the claims file defines them (see the section on the session definition below), HD information of the two halves of session 1 correlates with r = 0.761 over 323 WT cells (paper 0.90, lower bound 0.81) and r = 0.839 over 237 Fmr1-/y cells (paper 0.95, lower bound 0.855), so neither value is within tolerance. With H3026 left out the Fmr1-/y r is 0.869, within tolerance, and WT stays at 0.761; with the first day of each rat alone WT r is 0.650. With the 20 min sessions used in this section, WT r is 0.815, 0.005 above its bound, and Fmr1-/y r 0.835; with the first day alone WT r is 0.739. Spearman correlations with the 20 min sessions are higher (0.863 and 0.909). Five of the ten cells farthest from the diagonal are from H3026, the rat counted as Fmr1-/y against the archive's label. The 20 min cut was adopted after the first round of verification and departs from the claims file, so the outcome follows the claims file's definition.

fig1h-juvenile-smaller-offset¶

Within a session, the tuning curves of juvenile Fmr1-/y cells drift less relative to the room than those of WT cells; the angular offset between the two halves is smaller.

Result: reproduced. The offset between the two halves' tuning curves is smaller in juvenile Fmr1-/y cells (median 7 against 26 degrees; LME p = 0.035). It holds with the first day alone (p = 0.017), and not for cells with half-width below 120 degrees (p = 0.060), on rat means (t(10) = -2.09, p = 0.063), with H3026 left out (p = 0.068) or with the archive's labels (p = 0.17). With the claims file's session definition p = 0.014.

fig1j-juvenile-less-drift¶

Bayesian decoding shows less drift of the HD signal relative to the room in juvenile Fmr1-/y rats than in WT rats.

In [22]:
MIN_DRIFT_BINS = 300   # 1 min of decoded movement; a choice, shown as a variant


def drift_test(age, col):
    d = recs[(recs.age_group == age)].dropna(subset=[col])
    am = d.groupby(["subject", "genotype"])[col].mean().reset_index()
    ko, wt = am.loc[am.genotype == "KO", col], am.loc[am.genotype == "WT", col]
    t = stats.ttest_ind(ko, wt)
    return am, {"measure": col, "WT_mean": wt.mean(), "KO_mean": ko.mean(), "rats": f"{len(wt)} WT, {len(ko)} KO",
                "t": t.statistic, "df": len(am) - 2, "p": t.pvalue}
def drift_report(age):
    d = recs[recs.age_group == age]
    print("recordings without decoding (fewer than 6 cells):", d.loc[d.drift_mean.isna(), ["subject", "session", "n_cells"]].values.tolist())
    print("second-half bins of 200 ms: all, with valid tracking, with speed above 2 cm/s, and valid with speed above 2 cm/s (decoded and averaged):")
    print(d[["subject", "session", "genotype", "n_cells", "drift_bins_all", "drift_bins_valid", "drift_bins_fast", "drift_bins", "drift_mean", "drift_sd", "drift_mean_v2"]].round(2).to_string())
    rows = []
    for col in ("drift_mean", "drift_sd", "drift_mean_v2", "drift_sd_v2"):
        am, r = drift_test(age, col)
        rows.append(r)
    print("\nper rat (mean over recordings):")
    print(drift_test(age, "drift_mean")[0].round(2).to_string())
    print("\nt-tests on rat means (degrees):")
    print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string())
    first = recs[(recs.age_group == age) & recs.first_day].dropna(subset=["drift_mean"])
    ko, wt = first.loc[first.genotype == "KO", "drift_mean"], first.loc[first.genotype == "WT", "drift_mean"]
    t = stats.ttest_ind(ko, wt)
    print(f"variant, first day only: WT {wt.mean():.2f}, KO {ko.mean():.2f}, t({len(first) - 2}) = {t.statistic:.2f}, p = {t.pvalue:.4f}")
    arch_g = meta.set_index(["subject", "session_id"]).archive_genotype
    dd = d.dropna(subset=["drift_mean"]).copy()
    dd["genotype"] = [arch_g[(s, ss)] for s, ss in zip(dd.subject, dd.session)]
    am = dd.groupby(["subject", "genotype"]).drift_mean.mean().reset_index()
    t = stats.ttest_ind(am.loc[am.genotype == "KO", "drift_mean"], am.loc[am.genotype == "WT", "drift_mean"])
    print(f"variant, archive genotypes: t({len(am) - 2}) = {t.statistic:.2f}, p = {t.pvalue:.4f}")
    for name, sub in ((f"recordings with at least {MIN_DRIFT_BINS} averaged bins", d[d.drift_bins >= MIN_DRIFT_BINS]),
                      ("H3026 left out", d[d.subject != "H3026"])):
        if age == "adult" and name.startswith("H3026"):
            continue
        sub = sub.dropna(subset=["drift_mean"])
        am = sub.groupby(["subject", "genotype"]).drift_mean.mean().reset_index()
        ko, wt = am.loc[am.genotype == "KO", "drift_mean"], am.loc[am.genotype == "WT", "drift_mean"]
        t = stats.ttest_ind(ko, wt)
        print(f"variant, {name}: {len(wt)} WT, {len(ko)} KO rats; WT {wt.mean():.2f}, KO {ko.mean():.2f}, t({len(am) - 2}) = {t.statistic:.2f}, p = {t.pvalue:.4f}")
drift_report("juvenile")

Result: not reproduced. Decoder drift is lower in Fmr1-/y rats (rat means 17.0 against 35.0 degrees) but the t-test on rat means is not significant (t(10) = -1.91, p = 0.085). With version 2's 1.5 cm/s threshold p = 0.064, for the SD of drift p = 0.12, with the first day alone p = 0.088, with the archive's labels p = 0.20, with H3026 left out p = 0.14. H3019 (210618-1) is left out with 5 cells. H3001 (200201) is decoded on 279 bins, where the other recordings have 491 to 2480: only 330 of its 3000 second-half bins have a speed above 2 cm/s, though 2914 have valid tracking. Leaving out recordings under 300 bins gives p = 0.085.

figs1j-juvenile-epochs-correlation and figs1k-juvenile-epoch-drift-similar¶

In juveniles HD information is preserved between the two exploration sessions (WT r = 0.85, Fmr1-/y r = 0.85), and the drift of tuning curves between the sessions does not differ between genotypes.

Result: figs1j-juvenile-epochs-correlation partially reproduced; figs1k-juvenile-epoch-drift-similar reproduced. HD information correlates between the two sessions with r = 0.853 over 309 WT cells (paper 0.85) and 0.753 over 225 Fmr1-/y cells (paper 0.85, tolerance down to 0.765), so one of the two values is within tolerance. The offset between sessions does not differ between genotypes (median 14 against 21 degrees; LME p = 0.87; first day p = 0.72; archive labels p = 0.44).

fig2c-juvenile-isomap-wake-correlation and fig2d-juvenile-isomap-wake-sharper¶

In juveniles the HD information of tuning curves computed against the Isomap angle of waking population activity matches that of real HD tuning curves (WT r = 0.84, Fmr1-/y r = 0.92), and juvenile Fmr1-/y cells are better tuned than WT cells to this internal HD signal.

In [24]:
def iso_report(age):
    d = recs[recs.age_group == age]
    print("Isomap alignment with real HD (Rayleigh length of the error) per recording; recordings with fewer than 6 cells left out:")
    print(d[["subject", "session", "genotype", "n_cells", "iso_alignment", "iso_flipped"]].round(3).to_string())
    print(f"alignment range {d.iso_alignment.min():.3f} to {d.iso_alignment.max():.3f}")
    c = cells[cells.age_group == age]
    for col in ("iso_wake_info", "real200_info"):
        top = c.sort_values(col, ascending=False).groupby("genotype").head(3)
        print(f"three highest {col} per genotype:")
        print(top[["genotype", "subject", "session", "unit", "n_spikes_s1", "iso_wake_info", "real200_info", "hd_info"]].round(4).to_string())

# Isomap fitted on at most 3000 bins (as in the first round of this attempt), beside the fit on every bin used in
# the analysis, for the recording with the most cells in each age group
seed_of = {(m["subject"], m["session_id"]): k for k, m in enumerate(meta.to_dict("records"))}
fit_rows = []
for age in ("juvenile", "adult"):
    rr_ = recs[recs.age_group == age].sort_values("n_cells").iloc[-1]
    k = seed_of[(rr_.subject, rr_.session)]
    s_ = hdfx.load_session(assets.asset_id[k])
    sub_ = hdfx.analyse(s_, age, seed=k, fit_max=3000)["cells"].set_index("unit")
    full_ = cells[(cells.subject == rr_.subject) & (cells.session == rr_.session)].set_index("unit")
    for col in ("iso_wake_info", "iso_rem_info"):
        b_ = full_[col].dropna()
        a_ = sub_[col].reindex(b_.index)
        fit_rows.append({"recording": f"{rr_.subject} {rr_.session}", "age": age, "measure": col, "cells": len(b_),
                         "median_full": b_.median(), "median_3000_bins": a_.median(),
                         "r_full_vs_3000": stats.pearsonr(a_, b_)[0],
                         "r_with_real200_full": stats.pearsonr(full_.loc[b_.index, "real200_info"], b_)[0] if col == "iso_wake_info" else np.nan,
                         "r_with_real200_3000": stats.pearsonr(full_.loc[b_.index, "real200_info"], a_)[0] if col == "iso_wake_info" else np.nan})
    del s_
print(pd.DataFrame(fit_rows).round(3).to_string())

Result: fig2c-juvenile-isomap-wake-correlation reproduced; fig2d-juvenile-isomap-wake-sharper not reproduced. The HD information of Isomap tuning curves correlates with that of real-HD curves with r = 0.815 in WT and 0.910 in Fmr1-/y (paper 0.84 and 0.92). Isomap HD information is higher in Fmr1-/y cells (median 0.416 against 0.243 bits/spike) but the LME test is not significant (p = 0.056); no variant that keeps the rat is below 0.05 (log values p = 0.13, first day p = 0.15, archive labels p = 0.14, H3026 left out p = 0.075, rat means p = 0.089), and only the Mann-Whitney test on cells is (p = 0.0007). The direction matches the paper. The Isomap angle aligned with real HD with Rayleigh lengths of 0.21 to 0.90. Isomap is fitted on every bin; fitting it on 3000 bins, as in the first round of this attempt, raises the median Isomap information of H3026 211003 from 0.435 to 0.546 bits/spike (r = 0.987 across its cells), while in H4823 the two fits agree (0.360 and 0.359).

fig2g-juvenile-isomap-rem-correlation and fig2h-juvenile-isomap-rem-sharper¶

In juveniles the HD information of tuning curves computed against the Isomap angle of REM activity matches that of real HD tuning curves (WT r = 0.73, Fmr1-/y r = 0.90), and juvenile Fmr1-/y cells are better tuned than WT cells to the internally generated signal during REM.

Result: fig2g-juvenile-isomap-rem-correlation partially reproduced; fig2h-juvenile-isomap-rem-sharper reproduced. The HD information of REM Isomap tuning curves correlates with that of waking real-HD curves with r = 0.833 in Fmr1-/y (paper 0.90, within tolerance) and 0.831 in WT (paper 0.73, above the tolerance of 0.657 to 0.803). REM Isomap HD information is higher in Fmr1-/y cells (median 0.401 against 0.169 bits/spike; LME p = 0.045). The result is at the threshold: on log values p = 0.092, with the first day alone p = 0.16, with the archive's labels p = 0.25, with H3026 left out p = 0.095, on rat means p = 0.079; leaving out the REM intervals inside exploration sessions gives p = 0.045.

Result: fig4c-adult-isomap-wake-correlation partially reproduced; fig4d-adult-isomap-wake-similar reproduced. Isomap and real-HD information correlate with r = 0.945 in WT (paper 0.95, within tolerance) and 0.614 in Fmr1-/y (paper 0.90, outside). Isomap HD information does not differ between genotypes (median 0.279 in Fmr1-/y against 0.336 in WT; LME p = 0.79; rat means p = 0.80). The Isomap angle aligned poorly with real HD in H4822 (0.152), H4824 (0.224) and H4817 (0.386), the three Fmr1-/y rats with the largest decoder drift; the three Fmr1-/y cells with the highest Isomap information are from H4817 and carry little real-HD information (0.45 to 0.67 bits/spike).

fig4g-adult-isomap-rem-correlation and fig4h-adult-isomap-rem-similar¶

In adults the HD information of Isomap tuning curves from REM activity matches that of real HD tuning curves (WT r = 0.82, Fmr1-/y r = 0.80), and does not differ between genotypes.

Session definition of the claims file¶

The analysis above cuts every exploration session to its first 20 min. The claims file defines the sessions as the same tracking blocks but cuts only a block longer than 30 min, to its first 1300 s. This cell repeats the main test of every claim with the claims file's definition, beside the 20 min sessions used above.

In [34]:
def rule_tables(key):
    cr, rr = [], []
    for r in results:
        m = r["meta"]
        if r[key] is None:
            continue
        base = {"subject": m["subject"], "session": m["session_id"], "age_group": m["age_group"], "genotype": m["genotype"],
                "first_day": first_day[m["subject"]] == m["session_id"]}
        rr.append({**base, **r[key]["rec"]})
        c = r[key]["cells"].copy()
        for k, v in base.items():
            c[k] = v
        cr.append(c)
    c = pd.concat(cr, ignore_index=True)
    c["animal"] = c.subject
    return c, pd.DataFrame(rr)


def main_stats(c, rc):
    rows = []
    def lme(claim, age, col):
        d = c[c.age_group == age]
        coef, p, n = hdfx.lme_lrt(d, col)
        rows.append({"claim": claim, "quantity": f"{col}: LME coef KO-WT; p", "value": f"{coef:.3f}; {p:.4f}", "n": n})
    def rr(claim, age, x, y):
        d = c[c.age_group == age].dropna(subset=[x, y])
        for g in ("WT", "KO"):
            e = d[d.genotype == g]
            rows.append({"claim": claim, "quantity": f"r {g}", "value": f"{stats.pearsonr(e[x], e[y])[0]:.4f}", "n": len(e)})
    def rat_t(claim, age, col):
        am = rc[rc.age_group == age].dropna(subset=[col]).groupby(["subject", "genotype"])[col].mean().reset_index()
        ko, wt = am.loc[am.genotype == "KO", col], am.loc[am.genotype == "WT", col]
        t = stats.ttest_ind(ko, wt)
        rows.append({"claim": claim, "quantity": f"{col}: rat means t; p", "value": f"{t.statistic:.2f}; {t.pvalue:.4f}", "n": len(am)})
    for age, beh, met in (("juvenile", "figs1c", "figs1"), ("adult", "figs2c", "figs2")):
        for col in ("inactive", "centre", "active_speed"):
            rat_t(beh, age, col)
        for col in ("contamination", "mean_rate", "peak_rate", "vector_length"):
            lme(met, age, col)
    j = {"tuning": "fig1ef", "halves": "fig1g", "offset": "fig1h", "drift": "fig1j", "epochs_r": "figs1j", "epochs_off": "figs1k",
         "iso_r": "fig2c", "iso": "fig2d", "rem_r": "fig2g", "rem": "fig2h"}
    a = {"tuning": "fig3ef", "halves": "fig3g", "offset": "fig3h", "drift": "fig3j", "epochs_r": "figs2j", "epochs_off": "figs2k",
         "iso_r": "fig4c", "iso": "fig4d", "rem_r": "fig4g", "rem": "fig4h"}
    for age, n in (("juvenile", j), ("adult", a)):
        lme(n["tuning"], age, "hd_info")
        lme(n["tuning"], age, "half_width")
        rr(n["halves"], age, "info_half1", "info_half2")
        lme(n["offset"], age, "offset_halves")
        rat_t(n["drift"], age, "drift_mean")
        rr(n["epochs_r"], age, "hd_info", "info_s2")
        lme(n["epochs_off"], age, "offset_epochs")
        rr(n["iso_r"], age, "real200_info", "iso_wake_info")
        lme(n["iso"], age, "iso_wake_info")
        rr(n["rem_r"], age, "real200_info", "iso_rem_info")
        lme(n["rem"], age, "iso_rem_info")
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

Result. With the claims file's definition every recording's sessions differ from the 20 min sessions, by up to 463 s (session 1 of H3001 200201 lasts 1663 s), and session 1 holds the same cells. One main test changes its outcome. For fig1g WT r falls from 0.815 to 0.761 and Fmr1-/y r is 0.839, so neither value is within tolerance and the claim is not reproduced under the rule used for the correlation claims; the third round of verification agreed with this change of outcome. The other tests stay on the same side of their criterion: figs1c active speed p = 0.0504, fig1ef HD information p = 0.031, fig1h p = 0.014, fig1j p = 0.069, fig2d p = 0.079, fig3h p = 0.042, fig3j p = 0.023, and the correlations of figs1j, fig2c, fig2g, fig3g, figs2j, fig4c and fig4g keep the same values within and outside tolerance. REM Isomap information (fig2h, p = 0.045) is the same under both definitions, as it does not use the sessions and the cells are the same; its change from not reproduced in the first round came from fitting Isomap on every bin.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

Several juvenile results sit near the 0.05 threshold and depend on the grouping. HD information (fig1ef, p = 0.030), the offset between halves (fig1h, p = 0.035) and REM Isomap information (fig2h, p = 0.045) lose significance with the archive's labels and with H3026 left out; fig1ef and fig1h hold with the first day of each rat alone, fig2h does not. Waking (fig2d) and REM (fig2h) Isomap information fall on opposite sides of 0.05 (p = 0.056 and 0.045) with LME coefficients of 0.196 and 0.207.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The genotype of H3026 and the age group of H3029 are taken from the paper's unit counts, not from the archive; the archive's labels and the juvenile results with H3026 left out are shown as variants. H4825's file is a re-timed copy of H4824's recording, so the adult Fmr1-/y group has 5 rats where the paper has 6. Cells re-recorded on consecutive days could not be excluded (the files give no probe depth per day), so they are counted on each day; the first day of each rat is shown as a variant. Exploration sessions are taken from the tracking, as the epoch tables do not mark them reliably, and cut to 20 min, the paper's session length. This departs from the claims file, which cuts only blocks over 30 min, to 1300 s, and the change was made after the first round of verification. Under the claims file's definition fig1g has neither correlation within tolerance (WT r 0.761, Fmr1-/y 0.839), so its outcome is not reproduced, following the claims file; no other outcome changes. The LME is a random-intercept linear model on the raw values; the paper chose between linear, lognormal and gamma models by the data. The decoder follows version 2's Methods, as version 1 gives none. Contamination above 0.5 is excluded, reading the Methods' "below 0.5" as a slip. The offsets include weakly tuned cells; cells with half-width below 120 degrees are shown as a variant.

What was found about the dandiset. The archive's genotype of H3026 and date of birth of H3029 disagree with the paper's counts, which they match when H3026 is a juvenile Fmr1-/y rat and H3029 a juvenile WT rat; the birth dates of H3023 and H3026 are after their recordings, which gives them negative ages in the archive's asset metadata, and no NWB file sets the age. H4825's file holds H4824's recording, re-timed to H4825's epochs and clipped at its end, so one adult Fmr1-/y rat's data are missing. The units table has no cell type, quality or depth. The epoch and task tables mislabel or merge sessions in several files and one file has a single epoch. Two files give positions in pixels while stating centimetres, with head direction on another range; in the others y starts at exactly 0. One unit has unsorted spike times, and juvenile files repeat tracking timestamps. The archive's about field lists the Fmr1 protein under anatomy with the identifier of the disorder.
